rv.q: Ella Dawson (Rosalind Lailey) cleverly plays a quiet and empathetic barmaid who pines after Bob. And best of the bunch is the wily, mysterious and devilishly charming Ernest Eccles (Michael Maloney) - an impossible face not to recognize for any lover of detective dramas like Lewis, Silent Witness or Midsomer Murders on TV.

A particular highlight of the production is a dancing scene in which Bob and Jenny go out together at the Globe in the West End. The sequence offers a moment of movement within an otherwise oppressive world, providing a striking contrast to the difficulties which define their relationship.

Ordinary lives, fraught choices and the quiet tragedy of wanting more in a city whose narrow confines haven’t shifted in a hundred years. Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky offers a quietly devastating portrait of 1920s London – one that feels unsettlingly close to the present day.
Jordan Scowen is a likeable, flawed everyman in thrall to Jenny, as Bob, the slightly bewildered stand-in for Hamilton himself.

Indeed, the use of set, moving from the rafters to project a wave-like effect of the River Thames is an impressive touch and one which again reiterates the care the design of this production has to bring such an ambitiously large work to the stage. Meanwhile, the production also includes a subplot which floats between comedy and discomfort.
